title: Artificial Intelligence — Organisational AI Compliance and Governance Process Flow
subtitle: POPIA 4 of 2013 · EEA 55 of 1998 · LRA 66 of 1995 · National AI Policy (draft withdrawn April 2026; redraft pending) · ISO/IEC 42001:2023 · King V · EU AI Act where in scope · As at 19 October 2026

overview.summary: This flow tells a South African organisation what to do, by when, and who hands off to whom, from the moment someone proposes to buy, build or switch on an artificial intelligence (AI) capability until that system is retired and the lessons feed back into policy. It covers predictive and classification models, generative AI (text, image, code and voice), AI agents that take actions on a user's behalf, and automated decision-making in HR and customer processes. It is written for two kinds of organisation at once: the deployer, which uses AI built by others (for example Microsoft 365 Copilot, a recruitment screening platform or a credit-scoring service), and the developer or integrator, which designs, configures or builds AI for itself or for clients (for example agents built in Voiceflow or Microsoft Copilot Studio). Where the two roles carry different duties, the flow says so; Phase 3 has a separate build track (3B).

notes.heading: Legal status
notes.text: As at 19 October 2026 South Africa has no AI-specific statute and no binding national AI policy. Cabinet approved a Draft National Artificial Intelligence Policy for public comment on 25 March 2026 and it was published on 10 April 2026 (GN 3880, GG 54477), but the Minister of Communications and Digital Technologies withdrew it on 26 April 2026 after fictitious, apparently AI-generated citations were found in its reference list. An expert advisory panel chaired by Prof Benjamin Rosman was announced on 12 May 2026. The department told Parliament in May 2026 that it aimed to take a revised draft to Cabinet in November 2026 and publish it for comment in January 2027; in September 2026 the Minister moved the Cabinet target to the end of the 2026/27 financial year (March 2027), and no new comment date has been announced. Reporting in July 2026 indicates the redraft is likely to set national guidelines for sector strategies and to rely on existing regulators rather than create the seven new bodies the withdrawn draft proposed (not yet confirmed by the department). No AI Bill has been tabled. AI compliance in South Africa therefore flows from technology-neutral laws already in force: chiefly the Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (POPIA), the Employment Equity Act 55 of 1998 (EEA), the Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995 (LRA), the Consumer Protection Act 68 of 2008 (CPA), the Electronic Communications and Transactions Act 25 of 2002 (ECTA), the Cybercrimes Act 19 of 2020, the Copyright Act 98 of 1978, the Regulation of Interception of Communications and Provision of Communication-Related Information Act 70 of 2002 (RICA) and the Constitution. Standards and codes (ISO/IEC 42001, King V) and foreign law (the EU AI Act, where in scope) supply the management-system structure.

notes.heading: Figures and dates in force
notes.text: POPIA administrative fine: up to R10 million (s.109). Amended POPIA Regulations in force from 17 April 2025. Information Regulator eServices portal mandatory for security-compromise notifications from 1 April 2025. King V Code: financial years starting on or after 1 January 2026. EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) as amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, OJ 24 July 2026, in force 27 July 2026): prohibitions and AI literacy since 2 February 2025; general-purpose AI (GPAI) obligations since 2 August 2025; transparency duties (art. 50) since 2 August 2026; Annex III high-risk duties deferred to 2 December 2027; Annex I (product) high-risk duties deferred to 2 August 2028.

notes.heading: Labels used throughout
points: LAW = binding in South Africa now (statute or regulation).
Code = Code of Good Practice issued under a statute; must be taken into account (for example LRA s.203(3)).
CL = case law (court judgments); binding to the extent of the court's authority.
POLICY / DRAFT = government policy, draft policy or Bill; not binding. Build readiness; do not treat as a current legal duty.
STD = voluntary standard or code (ISO/IEC, NIST, OECD, King V). Binding only if the organisation adopts it, a contract requires it, or a listing or sector rule incorporates it.
FOREIGN = foreign law that applies only where the organisation is in its scope (for example the EU AI Act where an AI system's output is used in the EU).
BP = best practice or internal control; not a statutory deadline. Adopt it as policy so it binds internally.

notes.heading: Design principle
notes.text: Because no single statute governs AI in South Africa, the flow builds one gate-controlled life cycle and hangs every applicable legal test on the step where it bites. Where a stricter foreign or standard-based control is cheap to adopt and likely to become SA policy (risk tiering, impact assessment, human oversight, AI literacy, incident logging), the flow adopts it now as BP, so that the organisation will not need a redesign when the revised national policy or sector rules arrive.

notes.heading: Seven interpretation points that shape the flow
1. Technology-neutral law still bites
notes.text: POPIA, the EEA and the CPA apply to an outcome whether a person or a model produced it. "The tool did it" is not a defence: the responsible party (POPIA s.1) or employer (EEA s.5–6) answers for the result. Every AI use case must therefore be mapped to the human accountability it replaces.

notes.heading: 2. "Based solely on automated processing" (POPIA s.71)
notes.text: The protection applies to a decision with legal consequences, or that affects the person to a substantial degree, which is based solely on automated processing intended to profile the person (performance at work, creditworthiness, reliability, location, health, personal preferences or conduct). The Information Regulator has issued no guidance on s.71 as at the date of this flow (verify before adoption). The flow treats a human "rubber stamp" that does not genuinely weigh the output as not human involvement, which is the cautious reading consistent with comparable foreign law. Meaningful review means a competent person with authority to differ, access to the inputs and time to consider them.

notes.heading: 3. AI assessments of people are "similar assessments" under EEA s.8
notes.text: Psychological testing "and other similar assessments" of an employee are prohibited unless the test is scientifically shown to be valid and reliable, can be applied fairly to all employees and is not biased against any employee or group. "Employee" includes an applicant (EEA s.9). The flow treats AI CV ranking, video-interview analysis, game-based assessment and personality inference as similar assessments. The HPCSA-certification paragraph (s.8(d)), inserted by the 2013 amendment, is not in operation: in Association of Test Publishers of South Africa v President of the RSA [2017] ZAGPPHC 144 (North Gauteng High Court, 3 May 2017) (CL) the court declared Proclamation 50 of 2014 void to the extent that it brought the amended s.8 into force, so s.8 as it stood on 31 July 2014 applies (no reported appeal found). The s.8(a)–(c) tests apply and the employer bears the burden of proof.

notes.heading: 4. Deployer, developer and POPIA roles do not map one-to-one
notes.text: An organisation using its own data in a vendor's AI is the responsible party and the vendor is normally an operator (POPIA s.20–21). A developer that builds an agent for a client and processes the client's data only on instructions is an operator. A vendor that uses customer data to train its own models for its own purposes becomes a responsible party in its own right for that processing, which needs its own lawful basis. Phase 1 step 1.2 settles the role before anything else.

notes.heading: 5. EU AI Act reach
notes.text: The EU AI Act applies to providers placing AI on the EU market and to providers and deployers outside the EU where the AI system's output is used in the EU (art. 2(1)(c)). A South African organisation with EU clients, EU employees or EU-facing chatbots must check scope at intake (step 1.5). Otherwise the Act is a reference model, not law.

notes.heading: 6. The four risk tiers are an internal policy device
notes.text: "Prohibited, high, limited, minimal" mirrors the EU structure but is adapted to SA law (step 1.4). The tier decides how much assessment and which approver; it does not replace any statutory test.

notes.heading: 7. Generative AI output is unverified until a person verifies it
notes.text: South African courts have criticised practitioners for filing AI-generated fictitious authorities (Parker v Forsyth NNO, Johannesburg Regional Court, 29 June 2023; Mavundla v MEC: Department of Co-operative Government and Traditional Affairs, KwaZulu-Natal [2025] ZAKZPHC 2, 2025 (3) SA 534 (KZP), January 2025; Northbound Processing (Pty) Ltd v South African Diamond and Precious Metals Regulator, Gauteng Division, Johannesburg, case 2025-072038, 30 June 2025) (CL), and the withdrawal of the draft national AI policy shows the same risk at government level. POPIA s.16 (quality of information) also requires reasonably practicable steps to keep personal information accurate. The flow requires human verification of any AI output used externally, in a decision about a person, or in a legal, financial or safety document.

notes.heading: Roles used
notes.text: AI Governance Owner (AIGO, accountable executive or senior manager who runs the programme); AI Governance Committee (AIC, cross-functional: AIGO, IO, HR, Legal, IT security, business; chaired by an executive); Board or Exco (BOARD, including the Social and Ethics or Risk Committee); Information Officer and Deputy Information Officers (IO); HR and Employment Equity Manager (HR); Legal and Compliance (LC); IT and Information Security (SEC); AI developers and builders (DEV, internal or contracted); Procurement (PROC); Business Owner of the use case (BO); line managers (LM); staff users (USER); designated PDA officer (DO, see the GBS PDA flow); affected persons (data subjects, candidates, customers).

stages.title: Phase 0 — Readiness (standing obligations)
intro: Phase 0 has no case trigger. These controls must exist before the first use case is assessed, because every later step assumes a policy, an owner, a register and a scheme to classify against. Most organisations already use AI informally ("shadow AI"), so Phase 0 also includes discovering and registering what is already in use. For GBS and other builders, step 0.13 adds developer standards.

notes.heading: Staff obligations at this stage
notes.text: Read and acknowledge the acceptable-use rules; use only approved tools; complete AI literacy training; declare AI tools already in use when the register is built.

notes.heading: Hand-offs
notes.text: BOARD → AIGO (mandate and policy). AIGO → HR (training and acknowledgements). AIGO → PROC (no AI purchase without clearance). IO → AIGO (POPIA baseline). HR → union or forum (consultation).

notes.heading: Watch
notes.text: The biggest Phase 0 failure is an AI policy that ignores AI already switched on. Enterprise copilots inherit every permission a user has: if SharePoint or Teams sites are over-shared, the copilot will surface salary files, disciplinary records or client data to anyone who asks. Fix permissions and sensitivity labels before enabling a tenant-wide copilot.

stages.title: Phase 2 — Assessment
intro: Phase 2 is one combined assessment, the AI impact assessment (AIIA), which includes the POPIA personal information impact assessment so that the business sees a single document and a single residual-risk decision. High-risk use cases complete every module; limited-risk use cases complete modules 2.2, 2.4, 2.7, 2.9 and 2.11 (AIIA-lite), plus 2.3 and 2.8 whenever special or children's PI is involved or personal information leaves South Africa, because those are statutory tests that apply at every tier. The assessment is done on the system as it will actually be configured and used, not on the vendor's brochure.

notes.heading: Business owner obligations at this stage

stages.title: Phase 4 — Approval gate and deployment
intro: Phase 4 is the single go/no-go decision. Nothing reaches live personal data or real decisions without a signed go-live certificate at the right level. The gate checks that every condition from Phase 2 is met, that notices and the s.71 route are live, and that someone owns monitoring from day one.

notes.heading: Hand-offs
notes.text: AIGO → AIC (go-live pack). AIC → AIGO (certificate and conditions). IO → affected persons (notices). HR → candidates and employees (notices, review route). AIGO → BO (monitoring ownership).

notes.heading: Watch
notes.text: Notices that say "we may use AI" are not enough. Tell people what the AI does in their case, whether a person decides, and exactly how to ask for human review. If a candidate cannot find the review route, the s.71 safeguard does not exist in practice.

Affected persons at this stage. They have a right to be told their information is processed and for what purpose (POPIA s.18), not to be subject to a solely automated decision except as s.71 allows (s.5(g)), and to object on reasonable grounds to processing based on legitimate interests (s.11(3)).

stages.title: Phase 5 — Operation and monitoring
intro: Phase 5 runs for as long as the system is live. AI systems change after go-live even when nobody touches them: vendors update models, input data drifts, users find new uses, and staff stop checking outputs once they trust them. Monitoring therefore covers the system, its outcomes and its users.

notes.heading: User obligations at this stage
notes.text: Use the system only for its approved purpose; verify outputs before relying on them; record overrides; report errors, bias or strange behaviour through the channel.

notes.heading: Hand-offs

notes.heading: Watch

stages.title: Phase 6 — Incidents, complaints and decommissioning
intro: Phase 6 handles anything that goes wrong and the orderly retirement of a system. An AI incident includes a security compromise, a harmful or discriminatory output, a wrong automated decision, a hallucinated statement given to a customer, an agent that acted outside its limits, or a confidential-data leak through a prompt.

notes.heading: Hand-offs
notes.text: AIGO → IO (possible compromise). IO → Information Regulator and data subjects (s.22). SEC → SAPS (cybercrime). HR → affected employees and candidates (corrected decisions). AIGO → AIC (root cause, decommissioning).

notes.heading: Watch
notes.text: Do not delete the system or its logs in a hurry after an incident. The evidence is needed to correct decisions, answer the Regulator and defend claims. Contain first, preserve second, delete only when the matter is closed.

Affected persons at this stage. They may complain to the organisation and to the Information Regulator, refer an unfair discrimination dispute to the CCMA, or approach a court for damages under POPIA s.99.

intro: These events can occur at any time after go-live (and some during a pilot). Each is handled on its own clock while the system continues or is paused.

steps.label: P1

steps.trigger: Data subject asks for human review or objects to a decision
steps.action: Acknowledge; suspend reliance on the automated output for that person; competent reviewer re-decides with full information; explain the underlying logic in plain language; record outcome.

steps.label: P2
steps.title: Discrimination claim
steps.trigger: Candidate or employee alleges unfair discrimination by an AI-assisted process
steps.action: Preserve the AIIA, bias tests, logs and decision records; assess validity evidence; respond to the CCMA referral; consider suspending the tool. referenceTables.title: Master flow at a glance
intro: Every AI use case enters at Phase 1, whether it is a new purchase, an in-house build, a client project or a new AI feature switched on inside software the organisation already licenses. The risk tier decides the path: a prohibited use stops; minimal-risk tools take a fast track (register entry, notices, light sign-off); limited and high-risk uses go through full assessment, contracting and a formal go-live gate. Once live, the system is monitored until it is retired, and the parallel track handles events (objections, complaints, claims, compromises, misuse) whenever they arise. Lessons from every phase loop back into the Phase 0 controls, and any material change to a live system (new model, new data, new purpose) re-enters at Phase 1.

Read each phase column top to bottom to see who acts and who hands off; read each lane left to right to see one party's whole job across the life cycle. The AI Governance Owner lane is the spine: every other lane connects to it. The Information Officer and HR lanes carry the two heaviest legal tests (POPIA and the EEA). Affected persons appear at go-live (they must be told) and in operation (they can make representations and ask for human review). The P-events lane runs underneath from go-live until decommissioning.

intro: National AI Policy. Cabinet approved the draft for comment on 25 March 2026; published 10 April 2026 (GN 3880, GG 54477; comment deadline was 10 June 2026); withdrawn by Minister Malatsi on 26 April 2026 after fictitious citations were found (SAnews statement of that date). Advisory panel chaired by Prof Benjamin Rosman (Wits) announced at the budget vote on 12 May 2026. Target given in May 2026: revised draft to Cabinet November 2026, comment January 2027 (ITWeb, 26 May 2026); on 21 September 2026 the Minister said the draft would be ready for Cabinet by March 2027 (Daily Maverick), and the department has not announced a new comment date. TechCentral (29 July 2026) reports a "radical rethink" towards guidelines, sector strategies and existing regulators. The August 2024 National AI Policy Framework was a discussion document. Status: no binding national AI policy and no AI Bill. Re-check before adoption.

Information Regulator. No AI-specific or s.71 guidance found (none as at March 2026 per ITLawCo; none found in searches on 19 October 2026; re-check before adoption). A guidance note on personal information impact assessments is planned for 2026/27. The Regulator's current members' term ends in November 2026.

EU AI Act. Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI): published 24 July 2026, in force 27 July 2026. Annex III high-risk deferred from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027; Annex I to 2 August 2028; art. 50 from 2 August 2026, with art. 50(2) grace to 2 December 2026 for systems already on the market; art. 4 recast as a duty to take measures to support AI literacy; new art. 4a on special-category data for bias detection; new prohibition of non-consensual intimate imagery ("nudification") from 2 December 2026. Confirmed against White & Case, Hunton and Cuatrecasas summaries of the Official Journal text (validation, 19 October 2026).

Copyright Amendment Bill. The Constitutional Court delivered judgment on the President's referral on 26 June 2026 (Ex parte President of the RSA: In re Constitutionality of the Copyright Amendment Bill and the Performers' Protection Amendment Bill (CCT 306/24) [2026] ZACC 26): the fair-use and most exceptions were upheld, the educational exceptions in s.12D(1)–(5) were held unconstitutional, the equitable-remuneration provisions (ss 6A, 7A, 8A) were not decided, and the President may not sign until Parliament cures the defect. It is not law. Neither the Bill nor the judgment addresses text-and-data mining or generative AI, so there is no statutory safe harbour for AI training; GBS should not rely on fair use for training until the Bill is enacted and tested.

EEA s.8(d). Not in operation: Association of Test Publishers of SA v President of the RSA [2017] ZAGPPHC 144 (3 May 2017) declared Proclamation 50 of 2014 void to the extent it brought the amended s.8 into force; s.8 as at 31 July 2014 applies. No reported appeal found.

Cybercrimes Act s.54. Most of the Act commenced on 1 December 2021; the s.54 reporting duty had not commenced at the last confirmed report (2024) and no later commencement proclamation was found on 19 October 2026 (open item; re-check).
Joint Standard 1 of 2023 (IT governance and risk management, financial institutions) is relevant to AI in financial services; it commenced on 15 November 2024.

s.71 is narrow and untested. It covers only decisions based solely on automated processing and gives no definition of "substantial degree". AI that heavily shapes but does not formally make a decision may fall outside it. The revised national policy or a Regulator guidance note should clarify meaningful human involvement.

EEA s.8 was written for psychometric tests. Whether AI ranking and video analysis are "similar assessments" is unresolved by the courts. A Code of Good Practice on AI in employment under the EEA would help.

Computer-generated works. Copyright Act s.1 attributes authorship to the person who made the arrangements, but the Act does not deal with AI training or with outputs that lack human creative input. The Copyright Amendment Bill does not resolve this.

No regulator of record for AI. Until the revised policy assigns mandates, oversight will be spread across the Information Regulator, the Competition Commission, the National Consumer Commission, ICASA, the FSCA and PA and the Employment Equity enforcement system. Organisations should engage with sector regulators directly.

Liability for autonomous agents. ECTA s.20 deals with electronic agents forming contracts but not with agents that take operational actions. Contract terms (AI12) must allocate this risk until the law does.

Independent second-line validation on 19 October 2026 found 0 Critical, 2 Major, 10 Minor and 4 Improvement findings. All were implemented in this version. The key claims that were independently confirmed are the Draft National AI Policy dates (Cabinet 25 March 2026; GN 3880, GG 54477 on 10 April 2026; withdrawn 26 April 2026), Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 and its dates, and the Constitutional Court copyright judgment of 26 June 2026.
